topic: Day 2 · Hypoglycaemia I — Physiology, Recognition & Risk
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Diabetes & Endocrine Unit
speakerBio: Diabetologist who runs the trust's hypoglycaemia-awareness clinic and teaches every cohort the counter-regulatory ladder from the top rung down.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

03:40. A 74-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on gliclazide and a recently up-titrated basal insulin is found by the night nurse drenched in sweat, groaning, and unrousable to voice. She skipped supper because she "wasn't hungry." A capillary glucose reads 1.9 mmol/L. Her partner says she has been "a bit vague and quiet" for two days and has stopped feeling her old warning shakes. That single detail — the lost warning — is the thread that runs through this whole lecture. To understand why she nearly died silently, we have to understand the ladder of hormones the body climbs when glucose falls, and what happens when repeated hypos saw the bottom rungs off that ladder.

1 · 🧠 Why the brain is uniquely vulnerable

Every other organ can burn fatty acids or ketones when glucose is scarce. The brain cannot — the blood–brain barrier excludes long-chain fatty acids, and ketone adaptation takes days it does not have in an acute hypo. The brain consumes roughly 120 g of glucose per day, has almost no stored glycogen, and depends on a continuous arterial supply. Interrupt that supply for minutes and you get neuroglycopenia; sustain it and you get neuronal death. This is why the body treats a falling glucose as a genuine emergency and mounts a layered, redundant hormonal defence long before the patient feels anything.

The brain is an obligate glucose consumer with no fuel reserve — hypoglycaemia is, first and last, a threat to the brain.

2 · 🪜 The counter-regulatory hierarchy — a ladder, defended in order

Glucose homeostasis is not a single switch; it is a sequential, redundant cascade. As glucose falls, defences activate at progressively lower thresholds — the highest-glucose response fires first, the last-ditch response fires only when the patient is already in trouble. Learn the order and the thresholds and you understand both normal physiology and every failure mode that follows.

OrderResponseApprox. glucose thresholdWhat it does
1st↓ Endogenous insulin secretion~4.4 mmol/LThe first and most sensitive defence — β-cells switch off, releasing the brake on hepatic glucose output
2nd↑ Glucagon (α-cells)~3.8 mmol/LThe dominant acute counter-regulator — drives hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
3rd↑ Adrenaline (adrenal medulla / sympatho-adrenal)~3.8 mmol/LBack-up to glucagon; raises glucose AND generates the autonomic warning symptoms
4th↑ Cortisol & growth hormone~3.6–3.7 mmol/LSlower, sustained defence — limit glucose utilisation, support gluconeogenesis over hours
ThenSymptoms (autonomic)~3.0 mmol/LWarning layer — prompts the patient to eat
FinallyCognitive impairment~2.8 mmol/L and belowNeuroglycopenia — the defence has failed; the patient can no longer self-treat
💡 The order is the exam answer

Falling insulin → rising glucagon → rising adrenaline → then cortisol & growth hormone. Insulin suppression and glucagon are the front-line acute defences; adrenaline is the critical back-up that also produces the warning symptoms; cortisol and GH matter for prolonged or recurrent hypoglycaemia. Remember it as: "switch off the brake, then call glucagon, then call adrenaline, then send in the slow reserves."

🎯 The glucose ladder of thresholds

Counter-regulatory hormones start at roughly 3.8 mmol/L — well before you feel anything. Autonomic symptoms appear around 3.0 mmol/L. Cognitive impairment begins around 2.8 mmol/L and worsens below. There is a deliberate safety margin: the body defends glucose hormonally long before symptoms and long, long before the brain fails. Diabetes therapy erodes that margin.

3 · 🥊 Autonomic vs neuroglycopenic — two symptom families

Hypoglycaemic symptoms split cleanly into two mechanistic groups, and the split is clinically decisive. Autonomic (adrenergic/cholinergic) symptoms are generated by the sympatho-adrenal discharge — they are the warning. Neuroglycopenic symptoms are the direct consequence of the brain running out of fuel — they are the emergency, and by the time they dominate the patient often cannot help themselves.

Autonomic (warning)Neuroglycopenic (brain starving)
MechanismSympatho-adrenal activation (adrenaline, ACh)Direct CNS glucose deprivation
ThresholdHigher (~3.0 mmol/L)Lower (~2.8 mmol/L and below)
SymptomsSweating, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, hunger, tingling, pallorConfusion, difficulty concentrating, slurred speech, behavioural change, drowsiness, focal deficit, seizure, coma
RoleThe alarm bell — tells the patient to eatThe fire — the patient may be unable to act
Autonomic symptoms are the smoke alarm; neuroglycopenic symptoms are the fire already in the room.
⚠️ Why losing the alarm is catastrophic

Autonomic symptoms fire at a higher glucose than neuroglycopenia. If the autonomic warning is blunted (see section 5), the patient sails straight from feeling normal into confusion, seizure, and coma with no warning window in which to eat. The whole danger of hypoglycaemia unawareness is this loss of the buffer between "I feel shaky, I should eat" and "I cannot form a sentence."

4 · 🔺 Whipple's triad — proving it was really hypoglycaemia

A low glucose on a meter is not, by itself, a diagnosis — meters read low with poor technique, cold peripheries, or delayed analysis, and some people feel "hypo" symptoms at normal glucose. Whipple's triad is the classic rule for confirming true, clinically significant hypoglycaemia:

  1. Symptoms consistent with hypoglycaemia (autonomic and/or neuroglycopenic), AND
  2. A low plasma glucose measured at the time of those symptoms, AND
  3. Resolution of symptoms when the glucose is raised.
💡 Use Whipple's triad to avoid two errors

It stops you (1) over-diagnosing hypoglycaemia in someone with adrenergic symptoms but normal glucose, and (2) dismissing a genuine dangerous low as a meter artefact. In the investigation of hypoglycaemia in a non-diabetic — a very different work-up — the triad is what justifies going hunting for an insulinoma or surreptitious sulfonylurea use. In a known insulin/sulfonylurea-treated diabetic, don't wait to satisfy all three before treating: treat first, confirm after.

5 · 🔁 Hypoglycaemia unawareness — the vicious cycle, drawn out

This is the mechanistic heart of the lecture. Hypoglycaemia-associated autonomic failure (HAAF) is how recurrent lows teach the body to stop warning you. Follow the cycle step by step:

  1. A hypo occurs. The sympatho-adrenal system fires; the patient feels shaky and sweaty at ~3.0 mmol/L.
  2. Recent antecedent hypoglycaemia lowers the threshold for the next counter-regulatory response. The brain, exposed to repeated lows, adapts by up-regulating glucose transport and defends at a lower glucose next time.
  3. The adrenaline (and glucagon) response now fires at a lower glucose — pushed down below the threshold for cognitive impairment.
  4. So the warning symptoms now appear AFTER, not before, the brain is already impaired — or do not appear at all. The patient has impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia.
  5. Unwarned, the patient does not treat, so hypos become more frequent and more severe — which further blunts counter-regulation. Round and round.
🎯 Two hits, one spiral

In established type 1 diabetes there is often already a defective glucagon response (α-cell dysfunction develops within a few years). That leaves adrenaline as the sole remaining acute defence and the source of the warning symptoms. HAAF then blunts that too — so the patient loses both their back-up glucose defence and their warning simultaneously. This is why unawareness confers a roughly 6-fold higher risk of severe hypoglycaemia.

💡 The good news — it is reversible

HAAF is not permanent. Scrupulous avoidance of hypoglycaemia for 2–3 weeks restores counter-regulatory responses and symptomatic awareness in many patients. The therapeutic move is counter-intuitive: deliberately relax glycaemic targets and accept slightly higher glucose to break the cycle, then re-tighten once awareness returns. Structured education (e.g. DAFNE-style), continuous glucose monitoring with alarms, and reducing nocturnal insulin all help.

Recurrent hypoglycaemia is the cause of hypoglycaemia unawareness — and hypoglycaemia avoidance is its cure.

6 · 📏 Definitions & levels — speak the same language

The ADA/EASD international consensus grades hypoglycaemia by glucose and by clinical consequence. Learn these — they structure trials, audit, and handover.

LevelGlucoseMeaning
Level 1 (alert)<3.9 mmol/L (≥3.0)Glucose low enough to need attention — a warning value; treat with fast carbohydrate
Level 2 (clinically significant)<3.0 mmol/LLow enough to cause neuroglycopenia and serious harm — clinically important
Level 3 (severe)No specific cut-offSevere cognitive/physical impairment requiring assistance from another person to recover — defined by the need for help, not a number
🎯 Why <3.9 and not lower?

3.9 mmol/L is chosen because it is the approximate glucose at which counter-regulatory hormone responses begin and above which the healthy brain is safe — and because in a treated diabetic it flags that the defensive margin is being eaten into before symptoms or impairment. It is deliberately conservative: a value to act on, not to panic over. Level 3 is defined by the need for third-party help — that is the clinically meaningful watershed, independent of the exact reading.

7 · 💊 The at-risk drugs — insulin and the sulfonylureas

Hypoglycaemia in diabetes is overwhelmingly iatrogenic. The culprits are the drugs that raise insulin levels regardless of the glucose — they do not "know" the glucose is falling.

Drug classMechanismHypo riskKey traps
InsulinDirect exogenous insulinHighWrong dose/timing, missed meals, exercise, renal impairment (reduced clearance), stacking correction doses
Sulfonylureas (gliclazide, glibenclamide, glipizide, glimepiride)Close β-cell KATP channels → glucose-independent insulin secretionHigh — and prolongedLong-acting agents (glibenclamide worst), renal impairment (accumulation), elderly, missed meals; hypos can last many hours and recur
Meglitinides (repaglinide)Same channel, shorter actionModerateMeal-related; shorter but still real
Metformin, DPP-4i, SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA (alone)Do not drive glucose-independent insulinLow aloneRisk rises when combined with insulin/sulfonylurea
⚠️ Sulfonylureas are the quiet killers

Because they force insulin secretion regardless of glucose, sulfonylureas cause hypos that are prolonged and recurrent — the drug outlasts a single treatment. Glibenclamide (long-acting, renally handled active metabolites) is the most dangerous and is best avoided in the elderly and in CKD. A sulfonylurea hypo is never "one and done" — it demands admission and monitoring (session 10). Metformin and the newer agents rarely cause hypoglycaemia on their own; blaming them wastes time.

8 · 👥 Who is at risk — the high-risk populations

The same dose of insulin or sulfonylurea is far more dangerous in some patients. Impaired drug clearance, poor gluconeogenic reserve, and unreliable intake stack the odds.

  • The elderly — reduced counter-regulation, unreliable meals, polypharmacy, and a higher chance that neuroglycopenia is mistaken for a stroke or dementia. Over-tight targets in frail elders cause net harm.
  • Chronic kidney disease — the kidney both clears insulin and sulfonylureas and contributes ~40% of gluconeogenesis. CKD therefore prolongs drug action AND weakens the glucose-raising response — a double hit.
  • Liver disease — depleted hepatic glycogen and impaired gluconeogenesis; the liver is the organ glucagon acts on, so cirrhosis blunts counter-regulation.
  • Alcohol — inhibits gluconeogenesis (NADH excess from ethanol metabolism blocks the pathway); a binge on an empty stomach can cause profound, delayed hypoglycaemia, and blunts the warning and the response to glucagon.
  • Prior severe hypo / impaired awareness — the single strongest predictor of the next one.
  • Long-duration type 1 diabetes, recent tight control, sleep, exercise, fasting/Ramadan, malabsorption.
💡 CKD is the multiplier to fear

In renal impairment, reduce or avoid renally-cleared sulfonylureas (especially glibenclamide), anticipate insulin requirements falling as GFR declines, and loosen targets. A dose that was safe at eGFR 60 can be lethal at eGFR 20.

9 · 🌙 The nocturnal blind spot

Sleep is where hypoglycaemia hides. The autonomic warning that would normally wake and prompt eating is blunted during sleep, and the sleeping patient obviously cannot self-treat. Nocturnal hypos are therefore longer, deeper, and more often severe — and frequently go entirely unrecognised, presenting only as morning headache, night sweats, vivid dreams, or unexplained morning hyperglycaemia (a counter-regulatory rebound). Crucially, each unrecognised nocturnal hypo further blunts the next day's counter-regulation, feeding the HAAF spiral. Continuous glucose monitoring with nocturnal alarms is transformative here.

☠️ M&M — the silent night

A 58-year-old man with type 1 diabetes of 30 years' duration was admitted for an elective hernia repair. His notes recorded "hypo unawareness" but no one changed his regimen. On the ward his usual bedtime long-acting insulin was given at the usual dose, but his evening meal was small because he felt nauseated. Overnight observations were "routine" — no capillary glucose was checked between 22:00 and the 06:00 round. At 06:00 he was found unresponsive, cold, and incontinent, with a capillary glucose of 1.4 mmol/L and a witnessed tonic–clonic seizure. He was resuscitated with IV glucose but had a prolonged confusional state and an aspiration pneumonia, and his surgery was cancelled. Lessons: (1) his documented impaired awareness meant he had no warning symptoms to wake him — exactly the population in whom nocturnal glucose must be monitored; (2) a reduced evening meal with an unchanged bedtime insulin dose is a classic recipe for a nocturnal hypo; (3) "routine obs" that skip overnight glucose in a high-risk patient are not safe; (4) the whole event was predictable from the physiology — recurrent lows had already sawn off his warning rungs, and sleep removed the last one. The team treated a label in the notes as information rather than as an instruction to act.

10 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. The brain is an obligate glucose consumer with no reserve — hypoglycaemia is fundamentally a threat to the brain, which is why the body defends glucose so aggressively.
  2. Counter-regulation is an ordered ladder: ↓insulin (~4.4) → ↑glucagon (~3.8) → ↑adrenaline (~3.8) → ↑cortisol/GH (~3.6); symptoms at ~3.0; cognitive impairment at ~2.8.
  3. Autonomic symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations) are the warning; neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, seizure, coma) are the emergency — lose the warning and you lose the safety window.
  4. Whipple's triad — symptoms + low glucose + relief on correction — confirms true hypoglycaemia; but in insulin/sulfonylurea-treated patients, treat first.
  5. Hypoglycaemia unawareness is a reversible vicious cycle: recurrent lows blunt counter-regulation and symptoms; 2–3 weeks of scrupulous hypo avoidance restores awareness.
  6. Know the levels: Level 1 <3.9, Level 2 <3.0, Level 3 = severe, needing another person's help.
  7. Insulin and sulfonylureas (especially long-acting glibenclamide) are the culprits; the elderly, CKD, liver disease, and alcohol are the multipliers — and the night is the blind spot.

moderatorQs.q: Walk us through the counter-regulatory response to a falling glucose — in order, with thresholds. Which hormone matters most acutely, and which is the source of warning symptoms?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The defences activate in a strict sequence as glucose falls. First, endogenous insulin secretion is suppressed (around 4.4 mmol/L) — the most sensitive response, releasing the brake on hepatic glucose output. Next, at roughly 3.8 mmol/L, glucagon rises — this is the dominant acute counter-regulator, driving hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. At a similar threshold adrenaline rises as the critical back-up and, importantly, is the source of the autonomic warning symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations). More slowly, cortisol and growth hormone (~3.6–3.7) support sustained defence. Autonomic symptoms then appear around 3.0 mmol/L and cognitive impairment around 2.8. So: glucagon matters most for acutely raising glucose, but adrenaline is what warns the patient — which is why blunting the adrenaline response is so dangerous.

moderatorQs.q: Explain the mechanism of hypoglycaemia unawareness and why it is a vicious cycle. How would you reverse it?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Unawareness arises from hypoglycaemia-associated autonomic failure: a recent antecedent hypo lowers the glucose threshold at which the sympatho-adrenal (adrenaline) response fires for the next episode. That threshold is pushed below the threshold for cognitive impairment, so the warning symptoms now appear only after — or instead of before — the brain is already impaired. Unwarned, the patient fails to treat, so hypos become more frequent and severe, which further blunts counter-regulation: a self-reinforcing spiral, compounded in long-standing type 1 diabetes by an already-defective glucagon response that leaves adrenaline as the sole defence. The key point is that it is reversible: scrupulous avoidance of hypoglycaemia for 2–3 weeks — deliberately relaxing targets, reducing nocturnal insulin, using CGM with alarms and structured education — restores both counter-regulation and symptomatic awareness.

moderatorQs.q: Define the three levels of hypoglycaemia in the ADA/international consensus, and justify why Level 1 uses 3.9 mmol/L.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Level 1 (glucose alert) is a glucose <3.9 mmol/L (and ≥3.0) — low enough to require attention and treatment with fast carbohydrate. Level 2 (clinically significant) is <3.0 mmol/L — low enough to cause neuroglycopenia and serious harm. Level 3 (severe) has no glucose cut-off; it is defined clinically as severe cognitive or physical impairment requiring assistance from another person to recover. The 3.9 threshold is deliberately conservative: it is roughly the glucose at which counter-regulatory hormones begin to engage, so in a treated diabetic it flags that the defensive margin is being eroded before symptoms or brain impairment occur — a value to act on rather than to panic over. Level 3 is defined by need for help precisely because that, not a number, is the clinically meaningful watershed.

audienceQs.q: An elderly patient on gliclazide with a low glucose keeps dropping again after we treat them. Why, and does it change what I do?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Yes — it changes everything. Sulfonylureas like gliclazide force glucose-independent insulin secretion, and the drug (and in some cases active metabolites) outlasts a single treatment, so hypos are characteristically prolonged and recurrent. In the elderly and in renal impairment the drug accumulates, making it worse. Practically: this patient should not be treated once and sent away — they need admission, IV glucose, and monitoring for many hours (often overnight), because the next dip may come while no one is watching. That is quite different from a short-lived insulin hypo in a young person, and it is the topic that carries straight into the management lecture.

audienceQs.q: A patient tells me they used to feel shaky before hypos but now just go straight to confused. What's happening and what do I advise?
audienceQs.answerHTML: They have developed impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia — the autonomic (adrenaline-driven) warning that used to fire around 3.0 mmol/L has been pushed down below the level at which the brain is already impaired, so the first thing they notice is neuroglycopenia (confusion) with no shaky warning window. The cause is recurrent hypoglycaemia, and the crucial message is that it is reversible: aim for strict avoidance of any hypoglycaemia for 2–3 weeks, which usually restores the warnings. Practically that means relaxing glucose targets, reducing nocturnal and pre-exercise insulin, using CGM with low-glucose alarms, and reviewing the regimen. Also flag the DVLA implications — impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia is a bar to driving until awareness is regained.

audienceQs.q: Why are CKD and alcohol such big risk factors — is it just reduced drug clearance?
audienceQs.answerHTML: It's more than clearance, and that's the teaching point. CKD is a double hit: the kidney clears insulin and sulfonylureas (so they accumulate and act longer) and the kidney normally contributes around 40% of gluconeogenesis (so the glucose-raising response is itself weakened). Expect insulin requirements to fall as GFR drops, and avoid renally-handled sulfonylureas such as glibenclamide. Alcohol directly inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis — ethanol metabolism generates excess NADH that blocks the pathway — so a binge, especially on an empty stomach, causes profound and often delayed hypos, and also blunts the counter-regulatory and glucagon responses. In both cases the body can't mount the normal glucose-raising defence, so a 'usual' dose becomes dangerous.
